```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(TEMPO)
```

`TEMPO` gives R access to the Romanian National Institute of Statistics'
TEMPO Online database: roughly 1500 statistical matrices covering population,
labour, agriculture, trade, prices and more.

The database is an external service, so the chunks that need it are shown but
not evaluated when this vignette is built. The chunks that need nothing but
the package itself do run, so the output you see for them is real.

## A two-minute tour

```{r tour, eval = FALSE}
library(TEMPO)

# 1. Find a table.
tables <- tempo_search("unemployed", language = "en")
tables[, c("code", "name")]

# 2. Look at its structure, and its size, before downloading anything.
meta <- tempo_meta("SOM101E", language = "en")
meta

# 3. Pull the slice you need straight into a data frame.
unemployment <- tempo_get(
  "SOM101E",
  filters = list(
    Sex        = "Total",
    Counties   = "Cluj",
    Localities = "TOTAL",
    Periods    = grep("2024", meta$values$Periods$label, value = TRUE)
  ),
  language = "en"
)
head(unemployment)
```

The package has three entry points, in increasing order of commitment:
`tempo_toc()` and `tempo_search()` tell you what exists, `tempo_meta()`
describes one table, and `tempo_get()` or `tempo_bulk()` fetch data.

## Finding a table

Start from the table of contents. The default language is Romanian; set
`language = "en"` for English table names.

```{r list-tables, eval = FALSE}
tables <- tempo_toc(language = "en")
nrow(tables)
head(tables)
```

The result has a `name` and a `code`, plus a `comment` when the service
supplies one. Searching it is common enough to have its own function, which
accepts several patterns and searches every character column:

```{r search, eval = FALSE}
tempo_search(c("population", "migration"), language = "en")

# Reuse a table of contents you already hold rather than fetching it again.
tempo_search("population", toc = tables)
```

The service stores table names without diacritics, so search for the
unaccented spelling: `"sanatate"`, not the accented form.

### Where a table sits in the classification

Two routes give you the statistical domain, sub-domain and survey.

`tempo_hierarchy()` reads the service's own navigation tree. The branch
structure, currently 8 domains, 70 sub-domains and 262 surveys, arrives in a
single request:

```{r hierarchy, eval = FALSE}
branches <- tempo_hierarchy(language = "en", matrices = FALSE)
table(branches$level)
subset(branches, level == 1, select = c(code, name))
```

The service does not include matrices in that listing, so placing every matrix
in the tree costs one further request per survey. Those are issued
concurrently and cached, and the default `matrices = TRUE` does it for you:

```{r hierarchy-matrices, eval = FALSE}
tree <- tempo_hierarchy(language = "en")

# Where does one matrix sit?
tree[tree$code == "POP105A", c("level", "path")]

# Every matrix under one domain.
population <- tree[tree$is_matrix & grepl("POPULATIE", tree$path), ]
head(population[, c("code", "name")])
```

`tempo_toc(full_description = TRUE)` attaches the same three levels to every
row of the table of contents. It has to ask about each matrix in turn, so even
with concurrent requests and caching the first call takes a while:

```{r detailed-toc, eval = FALSE}
described <- tempo_toc(full_description = TRUE, language = "en")
head(described[, c("code", "Statistical_domain", "Last_update")])

# What has been revised most recently?
head(described[order(described$Last_update, decreasing = TRUE), ])
```

`Last_update` is a `Date`, so it sorts and filters directly. The service
embeds HTML links in its top-level domain labels; those are stripped from
every text column, and the URLs are kept in `Press_releases`.

## Looking before downloading

A TEMPO matrix can be very large: county-by-locality tables crossed with
decades of years run to millions of observations. `tempo_meta()` tells you
what you are about to ask for, in a single request.

```{r meta, eval = FALSE}
meta <- tempo_meta("SOM101E", language = "en")
meta
#> <tempo_meta> SOM101E
#>   A. SOCIAL STATISTICS > LABOUR FORCE > REGISTERED UNEMPLOYED
#>   language:    en
#>   last update: 2026-10-12
#>   full table:  88,663,248 cells, over 2,000 requests
#>                too large to fetch whole; select values with tempo_get()
#>   dimensions:  5
#>     1. Sex (3 values): Total, Male, Female
#>     2. Counties (43 values): TOTAL, Alba, Arad, ...
#>     3. Localities (3182 values): TOTAL, 1017 ALBA IULIA MUNICIPALITY, ...
#>     4. Periods (216 values): Year 2010, January 2010, February 2010, ...
#>     5. MU: Persons (1 value): Number of persons
```

Two things in that output are worth dwelling on. The table has 88 million
cells, so it cannot be downloaded whole and `tempo_bulk()` would refuse it.
And the unit of measure is a dimension of its own, `MU: Persons`, because that
is how the service models it; [tempo_tidy()] later moves it out of the data
into a `unit` column.

The components are there for programmatic use:

```{r meta-parts, eval = FALSE}
meta$dimensions      # one row per dimension, with how many values each has
meta$cells           # size of a full download
meta$requests        # how many HTTP requests that would take
meta$values$Years    # the selectable values, with the service's identifiers
```

## Getting data into R

`tempo_get()` sends your selection to the service and returns a data frame.
Dimensions you do not mention come back whole, which for a table like the one
above would be far too much, so name the ones that matter:

```{r get, eval = FALSE}
unemployment <- tempo_get(
  "SOM101E",
  filters = list(
    Sex        = "Total",
    Counties   = "Cluj",
    Localities = "TOTAL",
    Periods    = grep("2024", meta$values$Periods$label, value = TRUE)
  ),
  language = "en"
)
```

Taking the `Periods` labels from `meta` rather than writing them out is worth
the habit: it keeps the call working whatever format the service uses for
those labels.

Filter values are matched against the dimension's labels: first exactly,
ignoring case and surrounding space; then as a whole token, so `2024` finds
`"January 2024"`; and finally against the service's own numeric identifiers. A
value that matches nothing is an error that lists what is available, rather
than a quietly smaller result:

```{r get-error, eval = FALSE}
tempo_get("SOM101E", filters = list(Counties = "Atlantis"), language = "en")
#> Error: No value of dimension "Counties" matches "Atlantis". Available
#> values (first 10 of 43): TOTAL; Alba; Arad; Arges; Bacau; ...
```

Dimension names can be abbreviated, or given by position:

```{r get-naming, eval = FALSE}
tempo_get("SOM101E", filters = list(Count = "Cluj", Period = "January 2024"),
          language = "en")
```

## What tidying does

The CSV that TEMPO Online returns needs work before it can be analysed, and
`tempo_get()` applies `tempo_tidy()` by default. This chunk runs, so you can
see exactly what changes. It is the service's own layout, including a footer
line and an observation marked `":"`:

```{r tidy-input}
csv <- paste(
  "Judete,Ani,UM: Numar persoane,Valoare",
  "Cluj,Anul 2019,Numar persoane,1234",
  "Cluj,Anul 2020,Numar persoane,:",
  "Bihor,Anul 2019,Numar persoane,987",
  ",,,(c) INS 1998-2026",
  sep = "\n"
)
cat(csv)
```

```{r tidy-output}
tidy <- tempo_tidy(csv, code = "DEMO101A")
tidy
str(tidy)
```

Four things happened:

* the unit of measure moved out of the `UM:` column *header* into a `unit`
  column;
* `Valoare` became a numeric `value`, with `":"` mapped to `NA`;
* `"Anul 2019"` became the integer `2019`;
* the trailing copyright line was dropped, while the row whose observation is
  missing was kept, because its dimension columns are filled.

Sub-annual tables also gain a `Date` column, which is what makes them usable
in a time-series workflow without per-project label parsing. This is the
layout with a separate `Luni` dimension:

```{r tidy-monthly}
monthly <- paste(
  "Luni,Ani,UM: Numar,Valoare",
  "luna ianuarie,Anul 2024,Numar,10",
  "luna februarie,Anul 2024,Numar,12",
  "luna decembrie,Anul 2024,Numar,14",
  sep = "\n"
)
tempo_tidy(monthly)
```

Quarters and semesters are parsed the same way, in Romanian and English.

Many matrices, including `SOM101E` above, instead use a single `Periods`
dimension whose labels mix frequencies. Those labels are left exactly as
received, because the label is the only thing separating an annual total from
a monthly figure of the same year, and `year` and `period` columns are added
alongside:

```{r tidy-mixed}
mixed <- paste(
  "Counties,Periods,UM: Persons,Value",
  "Cluj,Year 2010,Number of persons,100",
  "Cluj,January 2010,Number of persons,8",
  "Cluj,February 2010,Number of persons,9",
  sep = "\n"
)
tempo_tidy(mixed)
```

`period` is `NA` on the annual row, so `subset(x, !is.na(period))` gives the
monthly series and `subset(x, is.na(period))` the annual totals.

If a value cannot be read as a number, it is reported once with a warning and the
original text is kept in a `value_raw` column, so an unexpected flag becomes
visible instead of silently turning into `NA`:

```{r tidy-odd}
odd <- paste(
  "Judete,Ani,UM: Numar,Valoare",
  "Cluj,Anul 2019,Numar,1234",
  "Bihor,Anul 2019,Numar,confidential",
  sep = "\n"
)
suppressWarnings(tempo_tidy(odd))
```

Pass `tidy = FALSE` to `tempo_get()` to skip all of this and receive the
service's layout verbatim, every column a character vector.

## Downloading whole tables to disk

`tempo_bulk()` writes complete matrices as CSV files, which suits a pipeline
that reads the same tables repeatedly or needs them outside R.

```{r bulk, eval = FALSE}
data_directory <- file.path(tempdir(), "tempo-data")

files <- tempo_bulk(
  codes = c("ACC101B", "ACC101C"),
  language = "en",
  directory = data_directory
)

files
attr(files, "downloaded")
attr(files, "reason")
```

The return value names every requested matrix, whether or not it was fetched
in this call, so the path is always available:

```{r bulk-read, eval = FALSE}
accidents <- tempo_tidy(files[["ACC101B"]], code = "ACC101B")
```

### Reusing local files correctly

Next to the CSV files, `tempo_bulk()` keeps a `.tempo-manifest.json`
recording, for each file, the language, the service's own update string, the
retrieval time, the number of requests spent and an MD5 checksum. A file is
reused only when the language, the published revision and the checksum all
agree.

```{r bulk-incremental, eval = FALSE}
tempo_bulk("ACC101B", language = "en", directory = data_directory)
#> Skipping `ACC101B`: the local CSV is up to date.
#> All requested CSV files are up to date.

# Asking for the other language re-downloads rather than reusing the file.
tempo_bulk("ACC101B", language = "ro", directory = data_directory)

# Force a download regardless.
tempo_bulk("ACC101B", language = "en", directory = data_directory,
           overwrite = TRUE)
```

The manifest is also the provenance record for a reproducible pipeline: it
says which revision of each matrix your results were computed from, and when
it was retrieved.

## Large tables

The service will not answer an arbitrarily large query, so a download is split
into chunks whose product of selected values stays within
`getOption("TEMPO.max_cells")`, and the parts are concatenated. Each part's
CSV header is compared with the first part's, so misaligned columns are an
error rather than a corrupt file.

You rarely need to touch this, but the controls exist:

```{r options, eval = FALSE}
options(
  TEMPO.max_cells = 1e5,       # larger single queries
  TEMPO.max_connections = 2,   # gentler on the service
  TEMPO.throttle = 0.2         # at least 0.2s between requests
)
```

See `?"TEMPO-options"` for the full list. TEMPO Online is a small public
service with no published rate limit; the defaults are deliberately modest.

## Caching

The table of contents and the per-matrix metadata change rarely and are
expensive to fetch, so they are cached. By default the cache lives in the
session's temporary directory and disappears with the session:

```{r cache}
tempo_cache_dir()
```

To keep it between sessions, point it somewhere persistent:

```{r cache-persistent, eval = FALSE}
tempo_cache_dir(tools::R_user_dir("TEMPO", "cache"))

# Or, in a project .Rprofile:
options(TEMPO.cache_dir = tools::R_user_dir("TEMPO", "cache"))

tempo_cache_clear()
```

Observations are never cached; only metadata is.

## When the service misbehaves

TEMPO Online goes down, changes its response format, and occasionally returns
a 500 that succeeds on the next attempt. Transport failures and the statuses
worth retrying are retried with exponential backoff before an error surfaces
at all.

What does surface carries a class, so a script can tell a mistake of its own
from a problem at the other end:

```{r conditions}
tryCatch(
  tempo_toc(language = "fr"),
  tempo_input_error = function(condition) "my call was wrong",
  tempo_offline_error = function(condition) "the service is unreachable",
  tempo_error = function(condition) "something else"
)
```

```{r conditions-live, eval = FALSE}
# Read the HTTP status, and retry only what is worth retrying.
tryCatch(
  tempo_get("ACC101B"),
  tempo_http_error = function(condition) {
    message("HTTP ", condition$status_code, " from ", condition$url)
    NULL
  },
  tempo_offline_error = function(condition) {
    Sys.sleep(60)
    tempo_get("ACC101B")
  }
)
```

`?"TEMPO-conditions"` lists every class and the fields it carries. A plain
`tryCatch(expr, error = ...)` still catches all of them.

## Moving from version 0.1.0

The 0.1.0 API still works. Two behaviours changed on purpose:

* `tempo_bulk()` now returns the paths of **all** requested matrices, named by
  code, rather than only the newly written ones. Code that looped over the
  result still works; code that relied on skipped files being absent should
  consult `attr(files, "downloaded")`.
* `tempo_toc(full_description = TRUE)` returns `Last_update` as a `Date`
  instead of a character string, and its `Statistical_domain` no longer
  contains raw HTML.

Everything else is new: `tempo_get()`, `tempo_meta()`, `tempo_tidy()`,
`tempo_search()`, `tempo_hierarchy()`, `tempo_cache_dir()`.
